part.reserve.title: Spare tempo
part.reserve.summary: A pawn advance that does not harm the position passes the turn without moving the kings: with it, the opposition changes hands.
ex.e14: Play White and find the best move. In this 1933 study by {{Nikolai Grigoriev|nikolai-grigoriev}}, Black keeps a pawn advance in reserve to change the turn. Preserve your pawns and choose the waiting moves that still work after that reserve is spent.
ex.e14.hint:
With the black king on b4, you want yours on b2 with Black to move. Going to b2 at once gives Black the chance to answer with the pawn. Stay one step away from b2.

These do not work either:

At move 1
Premature direct opposition can be undone by Black’s reserve; the correct waiting move must also keep the pawns protected.
If White played 1.Kb1?, Black would reply 1...Kc3 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Kb1 Kc3 2.b4 Kxb4.
If White played 1.Kb2?, Black would reply 1...d4 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Kb2 d4 2.c3+ dxc3+.
If White played 1.c3+?, Black would reply 1...Kxc3 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.c3+ Kxc3 2.b4 Kxb4.

At move 2
Waiting is not just any retreat: the king must continue defending the structure, especially the c2-pawn.
If White played 2.Ka2?, Black would reply 2...Kxc2 and win. The line would be 2.Ka2 Kxc2 3.Ka3 d4.

At move 3
Approaching before Black’s reserve is spent repeats the original problem: the opposing advance changes the turn.
If White played 3.Kb2?, Black would reply 3...d4 and hold the draw. The line would be 3.Kb2 d4 4.c3+ dxc3+.

At move 5
The b3-pawn must be preserved as a future promotion candidate. Advancing it allows a capture; in the continuation below, the final capture on c3 is en passant, immediately after White’s two-square pawn advance.
If White played 5.b4?, Black would reply 5...Kxb4 and hold the draw. The line would be 5.b4 Kxb4 6.c4 dxc3.

At move 6
The black pawn’s threat must be dealt with without losing the pawn that will sustain the win. A king move can allow a capture with check.
If White played 6.b4?, Black would reply 6...Kxb4 and hold the draw. The line would be 6.b4 Kxb4 7.cxd3 Kc3.
If White played 6.Kd1?, Black would reply 6...dxc2+ and win. The line would be 6.Kd1 dxc2+ 7.Kc1 Kxb3.

At move 7
After the simplification, the king must support the pawn before it advances.
If White played 7.b4?, Black would reply 7...Kc4 and hold the draw. The line would be 7.b4 Kc4 8.b5 Kxb5.
ex.e14.solution:
1.Ka1!! 1.Kb2? is already direct opposition against the king on b4, but 1...d4! passes the move, and you are the one who has to give way. From a1, if 1...d4, 2.Kb2! and the opposition belongs to White. After 1...Kc3, 2.Kb1! After 2...Kb4, 3.Kc1 (a1 and a2 also do); after 3...Kc3, 4.Kd1! (or 4.Kb1). When the pawn finally advances, 4...d4 5.Kc1 d3 6.cxd3 Kxd3, 7.Kb2 places the king in front of the b3-pawn and preserves the win. On the first move, 1.Kb1, 1.Kb2, 1.c3+ and 1.c4 only draw.

ex.e15: Play White and find the best move. In this 1932 study by {{Nikolai Grigoriev|nikolai-grigoriev}}, the black king threatens to return to the queenside and capture your pawns. Coordinate the white king’s route with the available pawn advances until you obtain a useful entry.
ex.e15.hint:
Identify each king’s target, the squares that restrict their routes and the pawn advances still available. Following the opposing king helps only if it preserves your pawns and prepares an entry. Save the reserve until changing the turn improves that struggle.

These do not work either:

At move 1
The king must improve its position before the pawns move: spending a reserve early lets the black king approach along a route sufficient to draw.
If White played 1.b3?, Black would reply 1...Ke1 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.b3 Ke1 2.c3 Kd2.
If White played 1.c3?, Black would reply 1...Kf3 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.c3 Kf3 2.b3 Ke3.
If White played 1.c4?, Black would reply 1...Ke1 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.c4 Ke1 2.b3 Kd1.

At move 2
Now is the time to move the c2-pawn away from the opposing king while keeping its second step. Delaying this decision allows an effective king entry or pawn advance by Black.
If White played 2.Kf5?, Black would reply 2...Kd2 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Kf5 Kd2 3.c3 Kc2.
If White played 2.Kg3?, Black would reply 2...c4 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Kg3 c4 3.b3 cxb3.

At move 3
The king must follow upwards; changing the queenside structure or retreating loses control of when to use the reserve.
If White played 3.b3?, Black would reply 3...Kd3 and hold the draw. The line would be 3.b3 Kd3 4.b4 cxb4.
If White played 3.b4?, Black would reply 3...cxb4 and hold the draw. The line would be 3.b4 cxb4 4.cxb4 Kd4.
If White played 3.Kg3?, Black would reply 3...c4 and win. The line would be 3.Kg3 c4 4.Kf2 Kd3.

At move 4
The reserve still needs to be kept. Advancing the supporting pawn can allow exchanges that eliminate the advantage.
If White played 4.b3?, Black would reply 4...c4 and hold the draw. The line would be 4.b3 c4 5.bxc4 Kd6.
If White played 4.b4?, Black would reply 4...cxb4 and hold the draw. The line would be 4.b4 cxb4 5.cxb4 Kd4.

At move 5
Spending an advance before reaching the right position gives the black king time to return to the queenside.
If White played 5.b3?, Black would reply 5...c4 and hold the draw. The line would be 5.b3 c4 6.bxc4 Ke5.
If White played 5.c4?, Black would reply 5...Ke5 and hold the draw. The line would be 5.c4 Ke5 6.b3 Kd4.

At move 6
Moving one square higher does not solve the turn problem: the pawn reserve or the winning retreat must be assessed from the actual position.
If White played 6.Kg8?, Black would reply 6...Kf6 and hold the draw. The line would be 6.Kg8 Kf6 7.b3 c4.

At move 7
After spending the reserve, the outflanking opportunity must be used; returning to the previous plan can give back the draw.
If White played 7.b3?, Black would reply 7...Ke7 and hold the draw. The line would be 7.b3 Ke7 8.Kg6 Ke6.
If White played 7.Kg6?, Black would reply 7...Ke5 and hold the draw. The line would be 7.Kg6 Ke5 8.b3 Kd4.

At move 8
The king must enter the square that keeps the advantage in the struggle for the targets, not merely approach along the eighth rank.
If White played 8.Ke8?, Black would reply 8...Kd4 and hold the draw. The line would be 8.Ke8 Kd4 9.Kd7 Kxc4.
ex.e15.solution:
1.Kg4!, and after 1...Ke3, 2.c3! The pawn leaves the black king's reach and keeps its second step, c4, for later. The kings climb on the same rank, 3.Kg5 Ke5, 4.Kg6 Ke6, 5.Kg7 Ke7, with one square between them and White to move: the opposition along the rank is Black's. On the seventh rank, 6.c4! uses the reserve to change the turn without moving the kings. The retreat 6.Kg6 also preserves the win, whereas after 6.Kg8? Black draws by replying 6...Kf6. Being near the edge requires choosing the square and the turn carefully, rather than simply continuing upwards. After 6...Ke6, 7.Kf8! and 8.Ke7 go round the black king and reach the c5-pawn first. On the first move, 1.c3 allows 1...Kf3 with the opposition for Black; on the second, 2.c4 lets the black king come back.

The line would be 1.c3 Kf3 2.b3 Ke3. If White played 1.c4?, Black would reply 1...Ke1 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.c4 Ke1 2.b3 Kd1.

ex.e16: Play White and find the best move. In this 1929 study by {{Nikolai Grigoriev|nikolai-grigoriev}}, the black king can outflank on the queenside and threaten e5. Assess whether opposition on the central file is enough or whether you need counterplay elsewhere.
ex.e16.hint:
1.Ke2 would take the distant opposition, but the fight is not on the e-file: the black king will go round by the queenside to the e5-pawn. Think about your king's target and which square it must be on when the black king reaches e5.

These do not work either:

At move 1
Opposition in the centre does not protect the decisive objective. The white king must prepare kingside counterplay before the black king outflanks.
If White played 1.Kd2?, Black would reply 1...Kd7 and win. The line would be 1.Kd2 Kd7 2.Kc3 Kc6.
If White played 1.Ke2?, Black would reply 1...Kd7 and win. The line would be 1.Ke2 Kd7 2.Kd3 Kc6.

At move 2
The h7 target must be fixed before the approach continues. If the king moves, Black can prevent the same plan with a pawn advance or gain time on the queenside.
If White played 2.Ke3?, Black would reply 2...Kc6 and win. The line would be 2.Ke3 Kc6 3.Kd4 Kb5.
If White played 2.Kf3?, Black would reply 2...h6 and win. The line would be 2.Kf3 h6 3.Ke3 Kc6.
If White played 2.Kg3?, Black would reply 2...h6 and win. The line would be 2.Kg3 h6 3.Kf3 Kc6.

At move 3
If White played 3.Ke3? or 3.Kf3?, Black would reply 3...Kd5 and win: after 4.Kf4 Kd4, the kings stand on f4 and d4, on the same rank, with e4 between them and White to move. The lateral opposition belongs to Black: the black king controls e4, and the white king cannot cross that square.

At move 4
If White played 4.Kf4? or 4.Kg4?, Black would also win: 4.Kf4 Kd4 5.Kg4 Ke4 and 4.Kg4 Ke4 5.Kh4 Kf4 end with the kings on the same rank, one square between them and White to move. Reaching the fourth rank was not enough: in that confrontation it is the white king that has to give way, and the counterplay against h7 does not arrive.

At move 5
Entering g5 too early lets the black king capture e5 and then reach f6, blocking the route to the target.
If White played 5.Kg5?, Black would reply 5...Kxe5 and win. The line would be 5.Kg5 Kxe5 6.Kg4 Kf6.

At move 6
The timing of the entry matters: occupying g5 before Black’s capture does not produce the same opposition as occupying it afterwards.
If White played 6.Kg5?, Black would reply 6...Kxe5 and win. The line would be 6.Kg5 Kxe5 7.Kg4 Kf6.

At move 7
After e5 is captured, retreating abandons the counterplay; pressure on the fixed target must be maintained.
If White played 7.Kf3?, Black would reply 7...Kd4 and win. The line would be 7.Kf3 Kd4 8.Ke2 Ke4.
ex.e16.solution:
1.Kf2!! 1.Ke2? takes the opposition and loses: 1...Kd7!, 2...Kc6, 3...Kb5, and the black king goes round. 1.h6? loses to 1...Kf7. The white king's target is the h7-pawn: after 1...Kd7, 2.h6! fixes it, and the king heads for the kingside, always in step with the black king: 2...Kc6 3.Kg3!, 3...Kd5 4.Kh4!, 4...Kd4 5.Kh5!, 5...Ke4 6.Kg4!, 6...Kxe5 7.Kg5! In the last two moves the kings stand on the same rank, on the same rank, with one square between them and Black to move: the black king gives way, and the white one reaches f6 and the h7-pawn. If 1...Ke7, 2.Kf3!!, for the same reason. Every white move in the line is the only one that draws.

part.waiting.title: Waiting with kings
part.waiting.summary: If bringing the king closer stalemates the opponent, wait with the king; spend your pawn move only after he has spent his.
part.fixedTarget.title: Fix first
part.fixedTarget.summary: First blockade the pawn that would give the opponent a spare move: without it, the turn does not change, and your king reaches the defence in time.
part.secondReserve.title: Save a tempo
part.secondReserve.summary: A pawn on the second rank gives two waiting moves if it advances one square at a time; save the second for when the king needs to change the turn.
ex.e14.r1: 1...Kc3. The black king attacks the c2-pawn and keeps the d5-pawn in reserve, a move to change the turn whenever it suits Black. The white king has to protect c2 again.
ex.e14.r2: 2...Kb4. The black king retreats to b4, still holding the d5 reserve. This is a common trap: the natural 3.Kb2? takes the direct opposition, but 3...d4! passes the move, and you are the one who must give way; Black draws. 3.Kc1, 3.Ka1 or 3.Ka2 wins: the white king waits without spending the opposition too early.
ex.e14.r3: 3...Kc3. The black king returns to c3 and attacks c2 again. Black repeats the manoeuvre hoping for a slip; c2 is still protected, and the white king must keep answering without giving up the opposition.
ex.e14.r4: 4...d4. Black spends the reserve: the pawn advances and threatens to go on to d3 to trade off the c2-pawn. Now Black has no waiting move left.
ex.e14.r5: 5...d3. The pawn attacks c2 and forces the trade. After it, everything is decided by the kings' race for the b3-pawn.
ex.e14.r6: 6...Kxd3. The black king recaptures and aims at the b3-pawn. The win depends on the white king protecting b3 in time and then escorting the pawn.
ex.e15.r1: 1...Ke3. The black king runs towards d2 to attack the c2-pawn. This is a common trap: the natural 2.Kf5? takes the king to the centre, but 2...Kd2! attacks c2, and Black draws. What wins is 2.c3: the pawn advances one square before the black king arrives, and the second step, c4, is kept in reserve.
ex.e15.r2: 2...Ke4. The black king stands on the same rank as yours, with one square between them and White to move: this is the opposition along the rank, which stops the white king from advancing through the centre. White, however, still has the move c3-c4 in hand.
ex.e15.r3: 3...Ke5. The black king moves up as well and keeps the opposition along the rank; if the white king steps towards the centre, it answers face to face.
ex.e15.r4: 4...Ke6. One more step up, again with one square between the kings and White to move. The opposition is still Black's, but the room to climb is running out.
ex.e15.r5: 5...Ke7. The kings reach the seventh rank, with Black still holding the opposition. The black king has nowhere left to climb; think about how to change the turn without moving the kings.
ex.e15.r6: 6...Ke6. The reserve has been spent, and the black king turns towards the c4-pawn, by way of e5 and d4. This is a common trap: the natural 7.Kg6? faces the black king again, but 7...Ke5! goes on to d4, the c4-pawn falls, and Black draws. What wins is 7.Kf8: the white king goes round behind and returns to the centre along the e-file in time.
ex.e15.r7: 7...Ke5. The black king runs to d4, from where it will attack the c4-pawn. The white king has to return to the centre with gain of tempo; remember that the b2-pawn can still protect c4.
ex.e16.r1: 1...Kd7. The black king sets off for the queenside, to go round via c6 and d5 and attack the e5-pawn. Your king has another target, the h7-pawn, and must march there in step with the black king.
ex.e16.r2: 2...Kc6. The black king continues its detour, now heading for d5. With h7 fixed as the target, the white king heads for the kingside; each of its squares must correspond to the black king's square.
ex.e16.r3: 3...Kd5. The black king stands next to the e5-pawn and could already capture it. It prefers to wait, because the capture only wins if the white king is on a square that does not correspond to its own.
ex.e16.r4: 4...Kd4. The black king makes a waiting step, without capturing. It tests whether the white king knows the square that corresponds to d4; one move out of step, and capturing on e5 wins.
ex.e16.r5: 5...Ke4. Another waiting step, now to e4, still next to the e5-pawn. Once again, the white king must find the square that corresponds to this one.
ex.e16.r6: 6...Kxe5. At last the black king captures the e5-pawn and wants to go on to f6, towards h7, to defend it. The white king must block that path with the opposition.
title: Waiting moves
summary: Changing the turn with a spare pawn move or a king waiting move, to keep the opposition and force the enemy king to give way.
history:
In many pawn endings what decides is not who has the closer king, but who is forced to move first. A pawn that can still advance without consequences is a spare tempo: it lets you pass the move to the opponent. A king move that changes nothing, made only to wait, is a waiting move. Whoever can count these moves turns a seemingly equal position into a win or a draw.

The Soviet master {{Nikolai Grigoriev|nikolai-grigoriev}} composed famous studies on the theme in the early twentieth century, in which two pawns and two kings seem frozen and yet only one precise waiting move keeps the result.
practice: Now the real ending: king on e1, pawn on f3, and the black king on c8. Bring the king in front of the pawn, toward the key squares e5, f5 and g5, and use the opposition to reach one of them. Pick your pace and go.
key.grigoriev: A study by {{Nikolai Grigoriev|nikolai-grigoriev}}, from 1933. Black keeps the advance of the d5 pawn in reserve, a move to change the turn whenever convenient. White needs waiting moves that still work after the reserve is spent.
ex.e20: Play as White and find the best move. Both kings are on the kingside, far from the queenside pawns, and the b6 pawn can still advance. Choose the king route that saves the game.
ex.e20.hint: Do not rush for the pawn: take the king up one file and keep it side by side with the black king, always with one square between them.
ex.e20.solution: 1.Kh2! climbs the h-file. After 1...Kf2, 2.Kh3! keeps the kings side by side; after 2...Kf3, 3.Kh4! and, after 3...Kf4, 4.Kh5! As long as your king follows the black king like this, it cannot get in, and the draw is secured.
ex.e20.r1: 1...Kf2. The black king climbs the f-file, trying to get ahead.
ex.e20.r2: 2...Kf3. The black king keeps climbing, always one file beside the white king.
ex.e20.r3: 3...Kf4. The black king reaches the fourth rank, and the white king still follows it.
ex.e21: Play as White and find the best move. Each side has one pawn still to move and the kings are close. Think about who runs out of pawn moves to pass the turn.
ex.e21.hint: One side has a pawn move that can be spent now or later. Decide which side should spend it first.
ex.e21.solution: 1.b5! locks the structure and forces Black to spend the pawn move; after 1...b6, nobody has a free pawn move left. Then 2.Kd2! takes the king to the opposition; after 2...Kc4, 3.Kc2! and, after 3...Kb4, 4.Kb2! Your king follows the black king and the draw is secured.
ex.e21.r1: 1...b6. Black spends the pawn move it was saving; now only the kings can move.
ex.e21.r2: 2...Kc4. The black king climbs to c4, trying to enter through the centre.
ex.e21.r3: 3...Kb4. The black king goes to b4, aiming at the b5 pawn.
ex.e22: Play as White and find the best move. The black king is shut in on h7 and each side has an a-file pawn. Find the move that takes the reserve away from Black.
ex.e22.hint: Whoever can still move the a-file pawn has a reserve move. Stop Black from using theirs when it needs it.
ex.e22.solution: 1.a5! advances the pawn and takes away the pawn move Black would use to pass the turn. After 1...Kh8, 2.Kg6! and, after 2...Kg8, 3.Kf6! After 3...Kh7, 4.Ke7! The white king reaches the a6 pawn and the win is certain.
ex.e22.r1: 1...Kh8. The black king has only king moves; it goes to the corner.
ex.e22.r2: 2...Kg8. The black king steps out to g8, trying to reach f8.
ex.e22.r3: 3...Kh7. The black king returns to h7 and the white king enters via e7.
coach.allPartsDone: Now you know how to use a waiting move to hand the move back to your opponent. Shall we go to the final test?
ex.e17.hint: First bring the king to the centre. When Black takes the opposition you do not have to give way: there is a move that is not a king move and passes the turn.
ex.e17.solution: 1.Kd4! brings the king to the centre, on the fourth rank. After 1...Kd6, Black takes the direct opposition; that is why 2.e3! passes the turn with a pawn move. After 2...Ke6, 3.Ke4! hands the opposition back to you, and 3...Kf7 opens the way to 4.Ke5, one of the key squares of the e3 pawn. From there the win is technical.
ex.e17.r1: 1...Kd6. The black king takes the direct opposition, with one square between the kings, and it is White to move.
ex.e17.r2: 2...Ke6. The black king returns in front of the pawn, but no longer has the opposition: White spent a pawn move to pass the turn.
ex.e17.r3: 3...Kf7. With no pawn move left to pass the turn, the black king has to give way; stepping back to d7 would have the same effect.
ex.e17: Play as White and find the best move. Your king is behind the e2 pawn and the black king waits in front of it. Find the plan that wins.
ex.e23: Play as White and find the best move. The kings stand in front of the central pawns, and your king defends the e4 pawn. If it were Black to move, the black king would have to leave f4. Find the move that passes the turn without giving anything up.
ex.e23.hint: Any king move leaves the e4 pawn undefended. Look for a move that is not a king move: it works as a spare tempo.
ex.e23.solution: 1.b4! is the spare tempo: it passes the turn without moving the king. Now Black is in zugzwang. The black king cannot go to f5, which the e4 pawn controls, and any other square abandons the e5 pawn: after 1...Kf3, 2.Kxe5 and White wins. A king move such as 1.Kc4? or 1.Ke6? leaves the e4 pawn undefended, and 1...Kxe4 draws.
ex.e24: Play as White and find the best move. The black king is in the a8 corner, and the b6 pawn is close to promotion. Beware of stalemate: choose your king's square and wait for the right moment to advance.
ex.e24.hint: Coming too close takes away every square from the black king. Leave it one free square, and advance the pawn when the black king steps out of the corner.
ex.e24.solution: 1.Kc6! waits and leaves the black king the b8 square. 1.Kc7? is stalemate at once: the black king has no move, and the game is drawn. After 1...Kb8, 2.b7! advances with the black king out of the corner; after 2...Ka7, 3.Kc7! guards b8, and the pawn will promote. If 3.b8=Q+?, 3...Kxb8 captures the queen and draws.
ex.e24.r1: 1...Kb8. The black king leaves the corner by the only free square.
ex.e24.r2: 2...Ka7. The black king goes to a7, the only square it has left.
